findings.title: Date override on a day makes every slot available, skipping busy-time checks
findings.body: In `checkIfIsAvailable`, the new block sets `dateOverrideExist = true` for any date override whose date matches the slot's date, and then `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` returns early. This return happens *before* the `busy.every(...)` loop, so on any day that has a date override the function reports every slot as available and completely ignores existing bookings, external calendar busy times, event buffers and reserved (`selectedSlots`) entries. Any host with a date override can therefore be double-booked. The override check should only narrow availability, not short-circuit the busy evaluation.

findings.title: working-hours check rejects slots when a user has more than one availability block per day
findings.body: `workingHours.find((workingHour) => ...)` returns truthy as soon as *one* working-hours entry does not contain the slot, and the result is interpreted as "slot is outside of working hours" -> unavailable. A user whose schedule has several blocks on the same weekday (e.g. 09:00-12:00 and 14:00-18:00) produces two `WorkingHours` entries with the same `days`, so a 10:00 slot is inside the first and outside the second and gets dropped — all slots vanish for split schedules. The same happens for schedules that cross UTC midnight, where `getWorkingHours` emits two normalized entries covering the same days. The predicate must be "no entry contains the slot" (`!workingHours.some(contains)`), not "some entry does not contain it". Note this path applies to personal events too, because single-user events are treated as fixed hosts.

findings.title: Date-override check rejects slots when a date has multiple override ranges
findings.body: `dateOverrides.find((date) => ...)` returns truthy for the first override that does *not* contain the slot, and that result is treated as "slot is not within the date override" -> unavailable. Cal.com allows several time ranges for the same override date (and several hosts' overrides are flattened into the same array when a team event is evaluated per host). With two ranges on one date (e.g. 09:00-11:00 and 14:00-16:00), a slot inside the first range is outside the second, so the slot is rejected and every slot on that date disappears. The condition should be "none of the overrides for this date contain the slot".

findings.title: `end` is computed from the slot start, so the working-hours end boundary is never enforced
findings.body: `const start = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute(); const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` — both variables are identical; `end` was clearly meant to be the slot end (`start + eventLength`, or derived from `slotEndTime`). As written, the `end > workingHour.endTime` test only ever compares the slot *start* against the end boundary, so a slot that starts inside working hours but ends after them (e.g. a 60-minute slot starting 30 minutes before the day's end time) is accepted, allowing bookings that run past the host's availability.

findings.title: Slots that only partially overlap a date override are treated as inside it
findings.body: The override containment test marks a slot as outside the override only when `slotEndTime <= override.start` or `slotStartTime > override.end`. A slot that starts before the override start but ends inside it (slot 13:30-14:30 vs override 14:00-18:00) or starts inside but ends after the end (slot 17:30-18:30 vs 14:00-18:00) satisfies neither condition, so it is considered available. Combined with the early `return true` for `dateOverrideExist`, such partially overlapping slots are offered for booking outside the host's overridden availability. The correct test is `slotStartTime < override.start || slotEndTime > override.end`.

findings.title: Override date comparison mixes server-local and UTC dates
findings.body: `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` formats in the *server's* local timezone (plain `dayjs(...)`, no `.utc()`), while it is compared against `slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")`, which is in UTC (`slotStartTime = time.utc()`). On any deployment whose process timezone is not UTC the two dates can differ by a day, so date overrides are matched to the wrong day: overrides are either ignored (making unavailable time bookable) or applied to the neighbouring day. Use `dayjs.utc(date.start)` for the comparison. Tests run with TZ=UTC will not catch this.

findings.title: Dayjs objects compared with `===`, so the zero-length (whole-day unavailable) override branch is dead code
findings.body: `if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares two freshly created Dayjs objects by reference, which is always false. The intent (treat an override whose start equals its end as "unavailable all day") is never executed, so the handling of whole-day "mark unavailable" overrides depends on the later, unrelated comparisons. Use `.isSame(...)` (or compare `valueOf()`).

findings.title: Override timezone shift loses the day when it crosses midnight
findings.body: The new override conversion reduces the shifted instant to minutes-since-midnight via `hour() * 60 + minute()`. When `offset` (invitee offset minus organizer offset) pushes the override across a day boundary — e.g. an override 22:00-23:00 in the organizer's timezone viewed by an invitee 5 hours ahead — the computed `startTime`/`endTime` wrap around to small values and are applied to the invitee's *same* day, so the override's slots are generated on the wrong day. If only one of the two endpoints wraps, `endTime < startTime` and `buildSlots` silently discards the range (`if (start >= end) continue`), so the override yields no slots at all. The day offset produced by the shift has to be carried, not discarded.

findings.title: Missing `override.timeZone` silently falls back to the process/default timezone
findings.body: `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` is called with `timeZone` typed as optional (`timeZone?: string` in packages/types/schedule.d.ts). When a caller of `getSlots` passes date overrides without a `timeZone` (the type permits it, and only the slots tRPC router was updated to populate it), the dayjs timezone plugin falls back to the default/local timezone, so `organizerUtcOffset` is computed for the wrong zone and the override is shifted by an arbitrary amount instead of being treated as organizer-local. Either make `timeZone` required for date overrides or explicitly fall back to `organizerTimeZone` which is already passed into `getSlots`.

findings.title: No test for the PR's main fix: date overrides of fixed hosts in round-robin events
findings.body: The PR's primary claim is that date overrides of fixed hosts are now honoured for ROUND_ROBIN events (so slots where the fixed host is unavailable are no longer offered). The only new test added covers a single-user event with a different invitee timezone. There is no scenario with a ROUND_ROBIN event type, a fixed host carrying a date override and a non-fixed host available all day, which is exactly the behaviour added in `checkIfIsAvailable` and the riskiest part of the change (it currently also bypasses busy-time checks). Without such a test the regression this PR fixes can silently come back.

findings.title: toHaveTimeSlots matcher does not compare lengths, so the new assertion can pass with missing slots
findings.body: The matcher iterates `schedule.slots[dateString].map(...).every((actualSlotTime, index) => ...)` over the *actual* slots only and never checks that the number of returned slots equals `expectedSlots.length`. The new assertion for the Asia/Dhaka invitee would therefore still pass if the implementation returned only `08:30:00.000Z` (or any prefix of the expected list), which is precisely the kind of over-filtering the new date-override/working-hours code can cause. Add a length check to the matcher so the new timezone test actually guards against dropped slots.
